p69: 69.  The applicant complained that the same judge had sat both in the proceedings which ended in 1997 and in those at the close of which he was found guilty in 2007. He further submitted that he had been deprived of his right to present his closing arguments. He relied on Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention, the relevant parts of which read as follows:
p70: 70.  While observing that Judge M.K. had taken part in both sets of criminal proceedings in question at first instance, the Chamber considered that the first proceedings had not involved any assessment of the facts or any examination of the question of the applicant’s guilt, and that Judge M.K. had not expressed an opinion on any aspect of the merits of the case.
p71: 71.  The Chamber therefore found that there was nothing to suggest a lack of impartiality on the part of Judge M.K.
p72: 72.  As regards the applicant’s removal from the courtroom, the Chamber found that that measure had not violated his right to defend himself, since, firstly, he had twice been warned not to interrupt the prosecutor while the latter was presenting his closing arguments and, secondly, his lawyer, who had remained in the courtroom, had been able to present his own.
p73: 73.  The applicant challenged the impartiality of Judge M.K., complaining that the judge had first adopted, on the basis of the General Amnesty Act, a decision terminating the criminal proceedings against him, and had then taken part in the criminal proceedings at the close of which he had been convicted on some of the charges brought in the first proceedings.
p74: 74.  The applicant explained that on 19 March 2007, after several hours of hearing, he had no longer been able to control his reactions owing to his mental illness and diabetes. As no doctor had been present to monitor his condition, he had uttered incomprehensible words while the prosecutor was presenting his closing arguments, but he had neither insulted nor interrupted him. Contrary to the Government’s assertion, he had not been warned twice by the presiding judge before being removed from the courtroom. He had not been allowed to return to the courtroom when the time had come for him to present his closing arguments. The fact that his lawyer had been able to present closing arguments did not make up for his own inability to do so. In criminal proceedings the accused could confess or show remorse, which could be taken into account as mitigating circumstances, and defence counsel could not take his place in that respect. The applicant therefore considered that the trial court should have had the opportunity to hear him present his closing arguments himself.
p75: 75.  The Government conceded that Judge M.K. had taken part in both sets of criminal proceedings against the applicant. As regards the question of subjective impartiality, they considered that the applicant had not produced any evidence capable of rebutting the presumption of impartiality in respect of Judge M.K.
p76: 76.  As regards objective impartiality, the Government explained that the first proceedings had not involved any assessment either of the facts of the case or of the merits of the murder charges against the applicant. Accordingly, in those proceedings Judge M.K. had not expressed any view on the applicant’s acts capable of prejudging his conduct in the second proceedings. Moreover, the outcome of the first proceedings had been favourable to the applicant. It was only at the close of the second proceedings that a judgment on the merits had been adopted, comprising an assessment of the facts of the case and of the applicant’s guilt. In both sets of proceedings Judge M.K. had dealt with the case only at first instance, and he had not taken part in the examination of the case at the appeal stage in either set of proceedings.
p77: 77.  The Government submitted that the applicant had been informed of the charges against him and of the prosecution evidence. He had been represented by a court-appointed lawyer throughout the proceedings and, whenever he had disapproved of the way in which his lawyer was handling the case, another lawyer had been appointed. The applicant and his lawyer had had ample opportunity to prepare their defence and to communicate in confidence. They had both been present at all the hearings and had been given every opportunity to respond to the prosecution’s arguments.
